parrafos: The Lauca River Valley Cathedral geosite lies just over 7.8 km west of the village of Ancuta, in Parinacota Province. The most direct way to reach it, however, is to head south from kilometer 158 of international route CH-11 (12 km before Chucuyo), along route A-235 to Misitune, and then continue south on route A-245 to about 1.5 km before the junction with route A-243, where a turn-off leads closer to the geosite.

This geosite is an amphitheater-shaped section of the valley where, from the Pleistocene to the present, erosion has sculpted striking pillar-like structures. They formed through intense runoff over slopes made of a series of lake sediment layers of varying thickness and different shades of brown, interbedded with whitish layers of volcanic ash. This whole sequence of sediments and ash is grouped into the so-called Lauca Formation, dated between 6.2 and 2.6 million years ago, spanning the Late Miocene to Late Pliocene.

The Morro de Arica geosite is a coastal hill about 280 m high at the southern end of the city of Arica. Declared a National Monument on October 6, 1971, it marks the northern end of the Coastal Range in Chile and the beginning of the coastal cliff. Its rocks, assigned to the Camaraca Formation, are the oldest in Arica Province and, based on their fossils, date to the Middle Jurassic, roughly 170 to 163 million years ago.

The cliff, the result of uplift and erosion during the Pleistocene to the present, exposes a sequence of layers gently tilted to the east (15-20°), made up mainly of andesitic lavas interbedded with fossil-bearing marine sedimentary rocks. The whole sequence formed in a shallow marine environment, as shown by its fossils: bivalves, ammonites, echinoderms, corals and brachiopods, all marine organisms of shallow waters.

The source of the volcanic material lay close to the coast, as shown by rapid-cooling structures formed when the lava came into contact with seawater. Lavas with these structures are called pillow lavas because of their oval shapes, and they can be seen with the naked eye in the rocks of the Morro.
This geosite is the main symbol of the city and is visited by many tourists every year, both for its panoramic view of the city and nearby beaches and for its historical significance.

The Amuyo lagoons, near the village of Camiña, are the surface expression of a deep hydrothermal system in which high-temperature fluids circulate through highly permeable volcanic rocks of the Oxaya Formation, of Oligocene-Miocene age. This circulation dissolves certain minerals in those rocks and increases the salinity and the concentration of some elements and compounds in the fluids.

The rise of these fluids and the constant precipitation of salts during the Middle Miocene to the present have formed hot-spring rocks: thick crusts of very striking colors that give the lagoons their name. Depending on the fluid composition, the crusts can be yellowish-green, if rich in the mineral orpiment, or orange-red, if realgar is abundant. The continuous build-up of crusts has formed a dome about 400 m across that rises some 15 m above the Caritaya River.

These extreme and unique environments also host bacterial colonies that tolerate the lagoons' high temperatures and salt concentrations (the Red Lagoon reaches a maximum of 57 °C measured at 11 m depth). These bacterial communities, called thermophiles because of their tolerance to heat, build organic structures known as stromatolites and thrombolites. Since such organisms have existed on Earth for about 3,500 million years, studying the colonies at this geosite is key to understanding the origin and development of life on Earth and the possibility of extraterrestrial life.

Because of the unusual colors of their waters and deposits, their striking shape and their contrast with the dull surroundings, these lagoons are a ritual space for Indigenous communities, which has given rise to rich stories and imagery about them, and they are also a major local tourist attraction.

The Cerro Dragón dune, declared a Nature Sanctuary in 2005, is one of the most important and striking landforms in the arid landscapes of northern Chile. This coastal dune sits at the southern end of a narrow, rocky marine terrace, averaging about 52 m a.s.l., bounded to the east by a coastal cliff some 500 m high, and on which the city of Iquique has developed.

About 4 km long and between 150 and 550 m wide, it stands out for its sharp, elongated and winding summit ending in a high, pointed crest. These features are precisely what make it look like a reclining dragon. Today the dune has no active source of sand, such as a beach, so it is classified as fossil or relict.

It has been proposed that it originated during the Last Glacial Maximum, about 20,000 years ago in the Late Pleistocene, when sea level was some 100 m lower than today and exposed a platform about 5 km wide, whose sediments would have supplied the sand to build the dune.

Despite being a protected area, the urban growth of Iquique has endangered the integrity and very existence of the Cerro Dragón dune. Real-estate pressure, sand extraction for construction and recreational activities have fragmented the dune and degraded its original natural landforms.

The Pintados salt flat, 47 km south of Pozo Almonte, lies within the Pampa del Tamarugal National Reserve, created in 1988. It is located where the Central Depression meets the Coastal Range, at the northern end of the Pampa del Tamarugal. It is a fossil or inactive salt flat, since it receives no recharge from surface streams, and its age spans the Pleistocene-Holocene, from about 2.6 million years ago to the present.

The salt flat is made of salt crusts and minor amounts of fine sediment. The most common salts are sulfates (gypsum, anhydrite), carbonates, nitrates and halides (common salt), forming a surface crust disconnected from the deep groundwater. Chemical analyses of this groundwater show a predominance of sulfates and sodium, although in some areas chloride or bicarbonate, and magnesium or calcium, also prevail, especially toward the southwest of the salt flat.

On the eastern slopes of the Coastal Range, in the central-western part of the salt flat, are the Pintados geoglyphs, declared a Historic Monument in 1969. They include about 450 figures over 50,000 m2 along a 3 km stretch. They were made by pre-Hispanic peoples between 700 and 1500 AD, mostly by removing surface material to create contrast with the natural rock surface.
An interpretation center here provides information about the geoglyphs and the archaeological finds related to the pre-Hispanic peoples.

g06.nombre: Los Puquios of the Llamara Salt Flat
parrafos: Some 43 km north of the village of Quillagua, in a low-lying part of the Llamara salt flat, there are two lagoons, called puquios in the Quechua language, where groundwater emerges. The salt crust, of Pleistocene-Holocene age (from about 2.6 million years ago to the present), is made of various minerals, mainly gypsum, calcite and halite, consistent with the chemical analyses of the puquio brines. These show a predominance of dissolved chloride and sodium ions, as well as high concentrations of arsenic and boron.

Their location in the Atacama Desert, where the highest solar radiation on the planet is recorded, and their exposure to it cause these lagoons to have very high evaporation rates. They also host two complex communities of microorganisms: microbial mats and evaporitic domes, both made of gypsum salts and microorganisms that thrive under extreme environmental conditions.

The Llamara salt flat is one of the few places in Chile with this type of microbial community, and it has been studied from biological, hydrogeological and hydrogeochemical perspectives. These studies provide valuable information about life in extreme environments, shedding light on the origin of life on Earth. Today the salt flat's groundwater is exploited by the Sociedad Química y Minera de Chile (SQM) and is subject to a monitoring and early-warning plan so that extraction does not harm water levels in the puquios.

El Tatio is the most important and emblematic geothermal field in Chile and Latin America, and the third most important in the world, for its geological and hydrothermal features as well as its history and development. The field lies in the high Andes of the Antofagasta Region, at 4,290 m a.s.l., 65 km northeast of San Pedro de Atacama and 7 km from the border with Argentina.

It has many hydrothermal features, such as hot pools, boiling mud pots, fumaroles and hot springs. However, it is its geysers, or hydrothermal eruptions, that give this geosite its importance, as they represent 8% of all such features worldwide. The cyanobacteria colonies associated with the extensive siliceous sinter deposits also add great value to the world's geobiological heritage, making this field a unique place to study and understand the origin and evolution of life.

Its geothermal origin is linked to highly permeable volcanic rocks at depth, the Río Salado Ignimbrite and the Puripicar Ignimbrite, of Late Miocene (9 million years) and Early Pliocene (4.3 million years) age respectively, and to geological structures that formed a trap, or reservoir, in these rocks. This created a system in which fluids accumulate and circulate at high temperatures, reaching 280 °C at depth and 86 °C at the surface, at 4,200 m a.s.l. These hot fluids come from the Pastos Grandes and Cerro Guacha volcanic calderas, in Bolivian territory.

Because of its characteristics, El Tatio is regarded by the Atacameño and Quechua Indigenous communities as a sacred ceremonial site, a place where inner energies gather and through which the Earth expresses the fullness of life.

La Portada, one of the symbols of the city and region of Antofagasta, is a national tourist attraction declared a Natural Monument on April 3, 1990, for its spectacular scenery and biodiversity. It comprises an active cliff, beaches, islets, caves and sea arches; the largest arch is the most striking and gives the place its name.

The cliff and arches have been carved mainly in layers of sedimentary rock of the La Portada Formation, which formed by sedimentation in a sea that existed from the Middle Miocene to the Pliocene, roughly 14 to 2.5 million years ago. Judging by the fossils in these rocks (mollusks and foraminifera and, to a lesser extent, fragments of fish, birds and cetaceans), they formed in warm-temperate waters no deeper than 200 m.

Below them, visible in the coastal rocks and at the base of the cliff and arches, are rocks of the La Negra Formation, produced by volcanic activity in the area during the Jurassic, between 180 and 143 million years ago.

During the Pleistocene, tectonic forces uplifted these rocks, exposing them to wave erosion and, to a lesser extent, wind, and causing rockfalls in the sedimentary layers. The constant action of these processes has sculpted the coastal cliff and its striking arches, which exist because the sedimentary rocks forming them resist the waves less than the volcanic rocks at their base.

The geosite is well preserved and easy to access, with viewpoints, a trail and a site museum. Access to the trail and the beach is restricted because of the risk of rockfall from the cliff, which keeps retreating slowly and steadily.

This geosite is in the Lila hills, in the Sierra de Almeida, about 20 km south of the Salar de Atacama. Discovered in 1962 from aerial photographs, it is the only confirmed meteorite impact structure in Chilean territory and one of the few recognized in South America. It is also one of the best-preserved impact structures for its age, making it a natural laboratory for studying simple impact craters. From the crater there is a privileged panoramic view of the Andes to the east, the Salar de Atacama to the north, and nearby ravines with a rich high-Andean flora that adds to the scenic beauty.

The crater is semicircular, with an average diameter of 360 m and a maximum depth of 34 m. The meteorite that formed it is estimated to have struck 500,000 to 700,000 years ago, in the Middle Pleistocene, at a probable speed of 15 km/s, with a mass of 9,870 tonnes and a diameter of 13.4 m. The impact would have released energy comparable to 2.2 atomic bombs like the one dropped on Hiroshima.

Both the remains of the iron meteorite and the impact structures produced by its fall (impactites) have been removed during many tourist and scientific expeditions without any regulation or oversight, losing valuable information about this event. In addition, a lack of awareness of the scientific value of this geosite has led some visitors to drive into the crater, rapidly damaging its walls.

This geosite is an intrusive rock called tonalite with an unusual and fascinating spotted appearance, of great beauty and scientific interest, which is why it was declared a Nature Sanctuary in 1981. It is a small rock outcrop no more than 2 m high on Rodillo beach, 11 km north of the city of Caldera, with direct access, parking and a rest area.

The striking texture of this rock, part of an intrusive body called the Relincho Pluton, between 195 and 180 million years old (Early Jurassic), comes from a series of spheres averaging 6 cm across, called orbicules, formed by a particular arrangement of minerals as the magma cooled and crystallized. Orbicular rocks are rare and diverse, with only about a hundred described worldwide. The Antofagasta Region has two other examples, the Quebrada Las Ánimas Diorite and a granodiorite in the Lila range, but neither is as spectacular as the orbicular tonalite of Caldera.

The orbicules consist of a core and a shell. The core is a rock called quartz diorite, around which a shell of radially oriented minerals crystallized, including plagioclase, clinopyroxene and amphibole, which get smaller outward, giving way to a rim dominated by dark crystals. Finally, tangentially arranged minerals close off and separate the orbicule from the granodiorite that crystallized between the orbicules, which also contains large crystals of potassium feldspar and mica.
Its location, exposed to the waves and occasional vandalism, makes it a very vulnerable geosite, even more so since the passing of Don Hipólito Avalos, its lone caretaker for about 20 years.

This 370-hectare municipal park lies 6 km southwest of Bahía Inglesa and was declared a national public-use asset in 2007. It mainly exposes marine sedimentary rocks of the Bahía Inglesa Formation (Middle Miocene-Pliocene), and in particular a sub-unit known as Mina Fosforita, of Late Miocene age, about 7 million years old. These layers are notable for their high phosphate content and an impressive abundance of vertebrate fossils, which is why they are also called a bone bed.

The fossils of Los Dedos are the most studied in this formation, although most are scattered and fragmented. More than 70 fossil vertebrate species have been identified in the Mina Fosforita sub-unit, including cartilaginous fish (sharks, rays and chimaeras), bony fish, crocodiles, seabirds (penguins, albatrosses, boobies, cormorants, petrels, pelagornithids), marine mammals (whales, dolphins, sperm whales, seals, dugongs and marine sloths) and land mammals (capybaras).

Among the sharks, the teeth of Carcharocles megalodon stand out for their size, reaching more than 15 cm. This fauna is joined by microscopic protozoa (foraminifera), invertebrates (mollusks and echinoderms) and plant remains. Because of their abundance of vertebrate fossils, scientists have described these layers as an example of an "exceptional deposit" (Fossil-Lagerstätte).

This geosite, 12 km east of the village of El Tránsito, stands out for its spectacular orange to yellowish-brown rock layers. They are part of a sequence of sedimentary rocks, sandstones and limestones, belonging to the Lautaro Formation, which is rich in fossils. This unit dates from the Early to Middle Jurassic, 190 to 170 million years ago, when this area and much of what is now southern South America lay under the sea. These sedimentary rocks also crop out in Quebrada La Totora and the Copiapó River valley, north of Quebrada Pinte.

Among the marine invertebrate fossils are well-preserved brachiopods (rhynchonellids and terebratulids), gastropods (genus Lithotrochus), bivalves, crinoids and ammonites (Fanninoceras, Phymatoceras, Peydelia), which together are typical of the Early Jurassic. A collection of some of these fossils and rocks can be seen at Don Gabito's site museum, inside the ravine.

Pichasca Natural Monument, declared in 1969, is in the Hurtado River valley, 56 km north of Ovalle and 2 km from the village of San Pedro de Pichasca. It is rich in fossils, notably petrified araucaria trunks (Araucarioxylon pichasquensis) and the bones of titanosaurs (Antarctosaurus wichmannianus), a dinosaur 18 m long. Teeth and bones of sauropods and theropods have also been found, along with fragments of turtle shells, bivalves and gastropods. All these fossils are from the Late Cretaceous and occur in rocks of the Quebrada La Totora Strata, about 86 million years old.

There is also great archaeological wealth from the Molle culture, whose people lived here about 9,000 years ago. Arrowheads, rock paintings, basketry and food remains have been found in the rock shelter known as Casa de Piedra, a cave 10 m deep, about 80 m long and between 2 and 5 m high. The shelter formed because the rocks here resist weathering to different degrees. The cave roof is a nearly horizontal intrusive rock called a sill, much more resistant than the sedimentary rocks beneath it. This intrusive rock also shows column-shaped fractures formed as the magma cooled and solidified, called columnar jointing.

Fray Jorge National Park lies in the Coastal Range, 62 km west of Ovalle and about 90 km south of La Serena. Covering 143,000 hectares, it was declared a National Park in 1977 because of plant species typical of southern Chile (hygrophilous forest trees such as olivillo and canelo), which survive here thanks to the moisture from coastal fog (camanchaca).

The park's coastline stands out for its terraced landforms. These terraces formed as waves wore down granitic intrusive rocks of Late Triassic age (213-201 million years), of the Altos de Talinay Plutonic Complex, and Early Pliocene sedimentary deposits about 5 million years old, which is why they are called marine abrasion terraces.

The existence of at least five terrace levels along the coast of the Coquimbo Region records changes in mean sea level and the uplift of the Coastal Range over the last 2.6 million years (Pleistocene-Holocene). On the park's southern coast, especially at the mouth of the Limarí River, three of these terrace levels can be seen north and south of the estuary; they have been dated to 321,000 years (T2), 122,000 years (T4) and 6,000 years for the lowest and youngest (T5), at 10 m a.s.l., spanning the Pleistocene-Holocene.

The Quereo dunes lie 2 km south of Los Vilos, between the coastline and the foothills of the Coastal Range. Some areas are still active thanks to wind-blown sand from the beaches, although their origin goes back to the Late Pleistocene, probably more than 30,000 years ago.

Buried beneath them, these dunes preserve many paleontological and archaeological remains that give this geosite a unique heritage value. They include abundant extinct fauna such as artiodactyls, mylodons and gomphotheres, between 8,000 and 30,000 years old (Pleistocene-Holocene). Archaeological remains show that the area was inhabited by hunter-gatherers at least 13,000 years ago, in the Late Pleistocene, offering important clues about the early peopling of the Americas.

On the edge of this geosite, just north of Quebrada Quereo, human skeletal remains were found that are the oldest dated so far in South America, about 12,000 years old. The Quereo dunes link the story of human settlement with the extinct fauna that lived in northern Chile. Together with their environmental and scenic value, this makes protecting and conserving this geosite important.

Rano Kao volcano, one of the most important landscape features of Easter Island (Rapa Nui), is between 900,000 and 100,000 years old, that is, Middle Pleistocene. Together with the also ancient Poike volcano and the younger Terevaka, it forms a volcanic complex produced by a mantle plume (hotspot) in the oceanic crust. This process gave rise to Easter Island (Rapa Nui).

Besides its value for Rapa Nui culture, the Rano Kao crater is geologically and environmentally important. The crater, 1.6 km across and 200 m deep, holds a lake that is one of the island's most important freshwater reservoirs and a key site for reconstructing past environments from the sediments and fossils on its bed. This geological record, reaching back 37,000 years into the Late Pleistocene, shows a gradual change in climate: from colder, drier conditions during the last glacial period to the wetter, warmer conditions that persist today.
Near the crater, particularly on the outer slope facing southwest toward the islets or motus, stands the ceremonial village of Orongo, of great significance to Rapa Nui culture.
